mappings.note: Full account of Saha's model - what was dropped, what was kept, what it then explained - which is LO-7's three clauses at three-mark length.
Mathematics as a compact statement of how quantities relate, with a distance-time-velocity example - C5.2-LO-7. No symbol or unit convention is at stake, so LO-6 stays out.
Asks for a representation of the mask's interdisciplinary nature and why branches must be joined - LO-3's man-made-divisions claim plus its worked example.
Importance of approximations in early reasoning - intuition, error detection, reasonableness. LO-9, with no rate computation demanded, unlike the breath-volume and water-jug items.

A social-media claim assessed by scientific reasoning is LO-4 (scientific thinking outside science); the argument used - no physical, chemical or biological mechanism - is LO-6's measurable-evidence test.
Defines a prediction as a reasoned expectation (LO-7) and then asks why it is powerful, which the answer settles on confidence from matching outcomes (LO-8).
Heating water is traced through a chemical reaction and then physical heat transfer - one everyday activity needing two branches, LO-3.
First half defines what makes a prediction testable (LO-6), second half asks Varsha to reason from past data to a forecast (LO-7). Both halves are separately scoreable.
Part one is what a theory is and does (LO-4); part two is why it must stay open to challenge (LO-5). The item fails if either is missing.
Short-range reliability against long-range uncertainty in a sensitive system - LO-10. Distinct from LO-8 because no forecast is being checked after the fact.

Rebuts the claim that ignoring detail is a flaw - LO-7's 'states which details it ignores and why'. LO-8 is not needed because the argument is about necessity, not about a specific question setting relevance.
Reads a confidence-versus-time graph for a chaotic system - LO-10, with the graph making the decay of certainty the whole point.

Comparing how physics and biology simplify differently means the same object would be modelled differently depending on the question the field asks - LO-8 on top of LO-7. Not C5.2-LO-3: no single problem needs both fields here.
A flowchart of the whole systematic inquiry cycle sits at the competency; C7.1-LO-4 is added for the specific step the second half asks about, repeated observations becoming a stated regular pattern.
Etymology of c generalised to how scientific symbols originate - the 'arose from history and international agreement' clause of LO-6.
A flowchart of what follows a failed prediction - re-examine assumptions rather than discard the idea, LO-8 verbatim. Revisability (LO-5) is the consequence, not what the item asks for.
Chains a rate (breaths per minute), an assumed per-breath volume and a balloon comparison as the independent cross-check - all three clauses of LO-9 in one item.
Defines a principle as broad guidance (LO-4) and contrasts it with an equation, which is a compact statement of a relationship (C5.2-LO-7). The contrast is the whole question, so both are needed.

Both framing symbols at three-mark depth: compass gives choosing models (LO-7) and asking the right questions (LO-6); the magnifying-glass half falls back to the inquiry competency because no outcome names observation. Partly weak fit.
Seconds and metres used so that any scientist can compare the measurement - the 'uses SI units correctly' clause of LO-6. Terms are mentioned only in passing, so C7.1-LO-6 is not the target.
The textbook's three-step strategy ends in a rough estimate used as a plausibility check - LO-9, with the earlier steps only feeding it.
Argues the necessity of simplification by imagining its absence - LO-7 approached from the counterfactual side.
Science as a human activity driven by curiosity (C5.2-LO-5) whose evidence then refines what is believed (C7.1-LO-5). The continuous loop in the diagram is what brings the second code in.
The student must justify inclusions and exclusions against one stated purpose - a bicycle commute - so relevance is decided by the question, LO-8, resting on the LO-7 definition.
Part (a) is the full law/theory/principle discrimination with examples (LO-4); part (b) is why theories are never final (LO-5). Two separately marked halves, two codes.
